study_identification_part.si4_title: A normative modelling approach reveals age-atypical cortical thickness in a subgroup of males with autism spectrum disorder

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To apply normative modeling to parameterize cortical thickness in ASD as individualized metrics of atypicality relative to typically-developing age-related norms, and to isolate a subgroup with highly age-atypical cortical thickness.

rci9_quality_checking_detail.answer: Euler index used as quantitative proxy for segmentation quality; top 10% of subjects with extreme Euler index (>300) excluded; Euler index included as confound variable in all models; visual inspection performed for globally atypical individuals; mean framewise displacement included as confound
rci9_quality_checking_detail.reason: The paper extensively describes quality control procedures using the Euler index. Supplementary materials provide detailed information about QC procedures including systematic exclusion thresholds, group differences in Euler index (d=0.176 and d=0.187 for left and right hemispheres), and sensitivity analyses.
rci9_quality_checking_detail.supporting_text: To assess the quality of Freesurfer reconstructions we computed the Euler index. The Euler number is a quantitative proxy index of segmentation quality and has shown high overlap with manual quality control labelling. In the full sample we found a small but significant difference in both hemispheres (Supplementary Fig. 2) with the autism group having overall slightly worse scan quality (d = 0.176 and d = 0.187 for left and right hemispheres, respectively). Therefore, we chose to exclude the top 10% of subjects with an extreme Euler index (corresponding to a Euler index of ~300) and reran the Matchit genetic matching algorithm to check for matched samples. To further ensure adequate control for scan quality we included the index itself as a confound variable in all models.
rci9_quality_checking_detail.location: Bethlehem2020.pdf.md: Methods / Imaging processing and quantification, L111-137

caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: The w-score for an individual thus reflects how far away their CT is from TD norms in units of standard deviation... We used a cut-off score of 2 standard deviations (i.e. w >= 2 or w<= 2). This cut-off allows us to isolate specific ASD patients with abnormal CT relative to age-norms for each individual brain region. We then calculated sample prevalence (percentage of all ASD patients with atypical w-scores)... We also wanted to assess how many patients have markedly atypical w-scores (beyond 2 SD) across a majority of brain regions. This was achieved by computing an individual global w-score ratio

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear mixed effects models with site as random effect, age/sex/motion/Euler as covariates; FDR correction (q<0.05); Spearman correlations between w-scores and phenotypic measures (ADOS, SRS, SCQ, AQ, FIQ, Age); FDR correction across 6 phenotypes × 308 regions = 1848 tests; outlier removal analysis to assess outlier-driven effects; bootstrap permutation tests for w-score reliability
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Only a small subset (median 7.6% per region) of ASD individuals show highly age-atypical cortical thickness (|w| > 2 SD), and these outliers drive most small case-control differences; removing outliers reduces significant regions from 27 to 14.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Conventional case-control analysis revealed small differences in cortical thickness in 8.7% of regions (27/308), with 26 regions showing effect sizes <0.2 SD. However, when region-specific outliers (w-score > 2 SD) were removed, significant regions decreased to 14 (1.9-fold reduction), indicating that small on-average effects were primarily driven by a small subset of highly atypical patients. The median prevalence of outliers across brain regions was 7.6% (significantly higher than expected 5%, X²=3.85, p=0.049). Outliers were predominantly in the 6-20 year age range with median age 10.6-20.2 years. W-scores showed no regions surviving FDR correction for on-average ASD atypicality. Exploratory brain-behavior analyses revealed SRS associations primarily in lateral frontal and parietal cortex, while ADOS associations were in lateral and inferior temporal cortex—regions largely different from case-control findings. Only 14 individuals (2%) showed global atypicality (ratio >0.5 across brain regions), likely due to image quality rather than biology. Bootstrap validation confirmed high reliability with median 1 unreliable region per subject out of 308.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Cross-sectional design limits individual trajectory inference; missing early developmental and late adulthood periods; post-hoc multi-site collection with heterogeneous scanners and protocols; site effects explain ~15% of variance; potential site-age interactions; limited to IQ≥70; incomplete phenotypic data for outlier subgroup; age-binning provides static norms rather than trajectory-based estimates
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: There are a number of caveats to consider in the present study. First and foremost, the present data are cross-sectional and the normative age modelling approach cannot make claims about trajectories at an individual level... The dataset also presents a post-hoc collection of sites accumulated through the ABIDE initiative, whereby scanners, imaging acquisition sequences and parameters, sample ascertainment, etc., are highly heterogeneous. As a result, we observed that site had a large effect on explaining variance in CT... our current sample was matched on IQ and as a result excluded individuals with low IQ scores (<70). While higher IQ does not automatically imply higher overall functioning it does limit the generalisability of our findings to individuals with normal to high IQ.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Sex-stratified approach used due to known sex differences; females excluded from main analysis due to insufficient sample size after age-binning; extensive sensitivity analyses for motion and QC confounds; centile estimation validated LOESS approach (r=0.87 for ABIDE I, r=0.66 for ABIDE II); comparison with EU-AIMS LEAP study showed consistency despite methodological differences

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a foundational normative modeling paper in autism using LOESS regression. Analysis focused on males only (n=699 ASD, n=624 TD) due to sample size limitations for females after age-binning. The paper also analyzed volume, surface area, and gyrification in supplementary materials with similar findings (outlier-driven effects). Code and data are openly available on GitHub (https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.1325171). A 360-region HCP parcellation was also tested but results focused on 308-region parcellation. The study emphasizes moving beyond case-control approaches toward individualized dimensional analyses for precision medicine in ASD.
